name: InSight lander
mission: InSight (Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy and Heat Transport)
headline: It sat still for four years, listening to Mars shake, until dust smothered its panels
story: On 26 November 2018, InSight set down on Elysium Planitia, a flat plain just north of the Martian equator. Unlike a rover, it was never meant to move. Its robotic arm lifted a seismometer off the lander's deck, set it on the ground, and covered it with a domed shield against the wind and the cold.

For four years it listened. InSight recorded 1,319 marsquakes, and their echoes let scientists look inside another planet: a crust thinner than expected and a molten core about 1,830 kilometers in radius. Not everything worked. Its heat probe, nicknamed the mole, was meant to hammer five meters down but stalled at about 40 centimeters.

Dust slowly covered its solar panels. In April 2022 it took a last selfie, already coated red. Its final image, on 11 December 2022, showed the dusty seismometer dome. Four days later it fell silent. When Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed it in October 2024, the lander had turned the same reddish-brown as the plain around it.

facts.label: Heat probe ("the mole")
facts.value: Reached about 40 cm of a planned 5 m

facts.label: Last contact
facts.value: 15 December 2022; mission declared over on 21 December

images.caption: 24 April 2022, sol 1,211: InSight's final selfie. Its solar panels carry far more dust than in its first selfie, taken weeks after landing.
11 December 2022, sol 1,436: one of the last images InSight ever took. The domed shield over its seismometer sits on the plain, dusted the color of Mars.
23 October 2024, seen from orbit by HiRISE: the silent lander at center, now nearly the same reddish-brown as the ground. The dark halo blasted by its landing thrusters is fading.

model.description: InSight with its solar panels and arm deployed. Surface instruments and the lander's final dust-covered condition are not reconstructed.
